title: Adolescent suicide risk: means restriction (remove firearm)
vignette: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the office by his mother for follow-up. Over the past month he has felt hopeless and has told his mother he sometimes wishes he were dead. He drinks alcohol daily. He has no prior psychiatric hospitalizations. During the visit, his mother mentions that she keeps a loaded firearm on the nightstand by her bedside at home. In addition to arranging mental health treatment, which of the following recommendations is most appropriate to reduce this patient's risk of suicide?

clues.text: felt hopeless and has told his mother he sometimes wishes he were dead
clues.note: Hopelessness plus passive suicidal ideation in an adolescent are significant suicide risk factors that require active risk reduction. (Sensitive topic - addressed as clinical care.)
Daily alcohol use is an independent, modifiable suicide risk factor (disinhibition, worsened mood, impaired judgment).

clues.text: keeps a loaded firearm on the nightstand
clues.note: Access to a loaded firearm is the single most lethal and modifiable suicide risk factor; restricting access to lethal means is the highest-yield intervention here.

whatMatters: An at-risk adolescent (hopelessness, suicidal ideation, daily alcohol) with a loaded firearm at home: the most effective, evidence-based way to reduce suicide risk is MEANS RESTRICTION - counsel the family to remove or securely lock away the firearm (and ammunition). Answer A. Firearms make suicide attempts far more lethal, and restricting access reduces deaths.
strategy: Recognize that reducing access to lethal means is a proven suicide-prevention intervention. With a firearm in the home, advising secure removal/locking is the highest-impact action alongside mental health treatment. Reject vague reassurance, delayed follow-up, or addressing an unrelated medical issue - none reduces the immediate lethal-means risk.

options.text: Advise the mother to remove or lock away the firearm
Reassure that suicidal thoughts are a normal part of adolescence
Recommend the patient keep a daily mood journal
Schedule a routine follow-up visit in 6 months
Advise limiting screen time before bed

eliminations.label: Reassure that suicidal thoughts are normal - false reassurance
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: normalizing/minimizing the ideation. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it dismisses real risk and does nothing to reduce access to lethal means; suicidal ideation should be taken seriously, not normalized. ✅ Correct if: never - active risk reduction is required.

eliminations.label: Mood journal - not a means-restriction intervention
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a self-monitoring tool. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it may support therapy but does not address the immediate, highest-yield risk (firearm access). ✅ Correct if: an adjunct within established treatment, not the primary safety step.

eliminations.label: Routine follow-up in 6 months - too delayed
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: deferring reassessment for months. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: an actively at-risk patient needs prompt intervention and means restriction now, not a distant appointment. ✅ Correct if: a stable patient without acute risk.

eliminations.label: Limit screen time - irrelevant to lethal-means risk
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a general sleep-hygiene tip. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it does not reduce suicide risk or firearm access. ✅ Correct if: isolated sleep-hygiene counseling, not suicide prevention.

eliminations.label: Treat Lyme disease - unrelated condition (your pick)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: addressing an incidental/unrelated medical issue. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it has no bearing on the acute suicide risk; the priority is means restriction plus mental health care. ✅ Correct if: managing an actual active infection unrelated to this safety question.

reasoning: Adolescent with hopelessness + suicidal ideation + daily alcohol = elevated suicide risk
A loaded firearm in the home is the most lethal, modifiable risk factor
Restricting access to lethal means (removing/locking the firearm) is proven to reduce suicide deaths
-> advise the mother to remove/lock away the firearm; answer A
mechanism: Suicide prevention combines treating the underlying condition (here, likely depression with comorbid alcohol use) with reducing access to lethal means. Firearms are the most lethal suicide method - most firearm suicide attempts are fatal, and the impulsive nature of many adolescent attempts means that removing quick access to a highly lethal method during a crisis window measurably lowers death rates ('means restriction'). Evidence-based counseling therefore includes advising families to remove firearms from the home or, at minimum, store them locked and unloaded with ammunition stored separately, and to secure medications and other lethal means. This is done alongside arranging mental health evaluation/treatment and addressing modifiable factors such as daily alcohol use. False reassurance, self-help tips, delayed follow-up, or attending to an unrelated medical problem do not address the immediate lethal-means risk. (Sensitive topic: if you or someone you know is struggling, contacting a clinician or a crisis line is appropriate - I can help find resources.)

difficulty.label: 📚 Pure knowledge gap
difficulty.message: First Aid Psych > suicide risk factors (SAD PERSONS: prior attempts, alcohol, hopelessness, access to means) and prevention: means restriction (firearms/medications) reduces deaths.

difficulty.label: 🧭 Understanding the question
difficulty.message: The question asks for the highest-yield risk-REDUCTION step when a firearm is accessible - means restriction.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocabulary
difficulty.message: Unsure on means restriction, protective vs risk factors, or suicidal ideation vs plan? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🧲 Pulled by a distractor
difficulty.message: Reassurance, journaling, delayed follow-up, sleep tips, and treating an unrelated issue don't reduce lethal-means access.

difficulty.label: ✍️ Something else
difficulty.message: Bank: suicide prevention = treat the disorder + restrict lethal means (remove/lock firearms); take ideation seriously. Sensitive topic - resources available on request.
